paper.title: Improvements in the GISTEMP Uncertainty Model

project.title: How Sure Are We That It Was the Hottest Year?
project.question: Using NASA's GISTEMP v4 global temperature record and its published uncertainty, how confident can we be that a given year was the warmest on record up to that date, and how does that confidence change as the record gets longer?
project.hypothesis: Because recent years have smaller uncertainty and are separated by a long-term trend, the probability that a recent record year is the true record will be high but below certainty, and it will be lower when the top years are close together.
data: GISTEMP v4 global annual mean anomalies (NASA GISS)
GISTEMP total uncertainty for the global annual mean (NASA GISS)
risks: Data files are updated every month; record the download date and version you used.
Treating each year's error as independent is a simplification; say so in your limitations.
Results describe the global record only; they say nothing about any single place.

milestones.title: Explore the temperature record
milestones.deliverable: Notebook that plots the annual global anomaly since 1880 with its uncertainty band

stuck.label: I can't read the data file properly
hints: Open the file in a text editor first. Are there extra header lines or symbols where numbers should be?
Many climate tables start with a title line and mark missing values with a symbol. pandas can skip leading rows and treat chosen symbols as missing when it reads a CSV.

Skeleton:
```python
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv(___, skiprows=___, na_values=___)
print(df.head())
```

stuck.label: I don't know which column to use
hints: Your question is about whole years. Which column summarizes a full year rather than one month or season?
Tables like this often list one column per month plus annual and seasonal means. For year-to-year comparisons, the annual mean (January to December) is the usual choice.
Analogous example: a gradebook might list each test and a final average. To compare students across years you would use the final average column, not one test.

stuck.label: I'm not sure how to draw the uncertainty band
hints: For each year, what two values would mark the bottom and the top of the band?
An uncertainty band is drawn between the value minus its uncertainty and the value plus its uncertainty for each year. matplotlib can shade the area between two lines.

Skeleton:
```python
plt.plot(years, anom)
plt.fill_between(years, anom - ___, anom + ___, alpha=0.3)
plt.xlabel("year"); plt.ylabel(___); plt.show()
```

milestones.title: Measure trends
milestones.deliverable: Table and plot of linear trends for at least three periods, with a short explanation of the method

stuck.label: I don't understand what an anomaly is
hints: What reference period does the dataset compare each year with? Look for it in the file header or on the data page.
An anomaly is the difference between a value and an average over a reference period. Using anomalies lets stations at different altitudes and climates be combined fairly.
Analogous example: comparing your height growth since last year is easier than comparing raw heights across a whole class. Anomalies do the same for temperatures.

stuck.label: My trend depends on which years I pick
hints: Try two different start years for the same end year. What changes, and why might that be?
A linear trend is sensitive to the chosen period, especially to short periods and to unusual years at the start or end. Report the period with every trend and compare several periods.

Skeleton:
```python
for start, end in [(___, ___), (___, ___), (___, ___)]:
    part = df[(df.year >= start) & (df.year <= end)]
    slope = np.polyfit(part.year, part.anom, ___)[0]
```

stuck.label: I don't know how to explain my trend in words
hints: What are the units of your slope, and how could you turn them into a per-decade rate?
A slope from a fit of anomaly against year is in degrees per year. Multiplying by ten gives degrees per decade, which is how trends are usually reported.
Sentence skeleton for your report: 'From ___ to ___, the global annual anomaly rose at about ___ degrees Celsius per decade, based on a linear fit to annual means.'

milestones.title: Simulate the uncertainty
milestones.deliverable: Code that draws many possible temperature histories and a check that their spread matches the published uncertainty

stuck.label: I don't know how to simulate the uncertainty
hints: If a year's value could reasonably be a little higher or lower, how could you generate one plausible version of that value?
Monte Carlo simulation draws random values many times. Here, each simulated history adds a random error to every year, with the size of the error set by that year's uncertainty.

Skeleton:
```python
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
sigma = ___  # convert the published uncertainty to a standard deviation
sims = anom + rng.normal(0, ___, size=(___, len(anom)))
```

stuck.label: I'm not sure what the published uncertainty number means
hints: Does the data page describe its uncertainty as a standard deviation or as a confidence interval? Find the exact wording.
A 95% confidence interval for a normal error is roughly two standard deviations on each side. Converting the interval to a standard deviation is needed before you draw random errors.
Analogous example: if a scale is said to be within plus or minus 2 grams 95% of the time, its typical error is about half that. Apply the same reasoning to the temperature uncertainty.

stuck.label: How do I know my simulation is right?
hints: What should the spread of your simulated values for one year look like if the simulation is correct?
A good check is to compare the spread of simulated values for a few years with the published uncertainty for those same years. They should match closely.

Skeleton:
```python
for y in [___, ___, ___]:
    i = years.tolist().index(y)
    print(y, np.percentile(sims[:, i], [2.5, 97.5]), anom[i] - ___, anom[i] + ___)
```

milestones.title: Record-year probabilities
milestones.deliverable: Table of the probability that each record year was the true record so far, compared with the paper's approach

stuck.label: I don't know how to find the record years
hints: Walking through the years in order, when does a year count as a new record?
A record year is warmer than every earlier year. A running maximum gives, for each year, the highest value so far, and a year is a record when it equals that running maximum.

Skeleton:
```python
running = np.maximum.accumulate(anom)
record_years = years[anom == ___]
```

stuck.label: I'm not sure how to turn simulations into a probability
hints: In a single simulated history, how would you check whether a given year is still the warmest so far?
For each simulated history, test whether the chosen year beats every earlier year. The share of histories where it does is the estimated probability.

Skeleton:
```python
i = ___  # index of the record year
wins = (sims[:, i] > sims[:, :i].max(axis=1)).mean()
```

stuck.label: My numbers differ from the paper
hints: List every choice you made that the paper might have made differently, such as the data version or how errors in different years relate.
Differences can come from newer data versions, independent versus correlated errors between years, or how the uncertainty was converted. Explaining a difference is part of good research.
Table skeleton for your report: choice | your project | the paper | could it change the result? Fill one row for data version, error model and number of simulations.

milestones.title: Write the report
milestones.deliverable: 4-page report: question, data, method, results, limitations

stuck.label: I don't know how to structure the report
hints: Could a classmate repeat your work from the report alone? What would they still need to ask you?
A short research report usually has a question, data and method, results with one main figure and one table, discussion, and limitations. The paper you started from follows a similar order.
Outline skeleton: 1. Question, 2. Data (GISTEMP v4, download date), 3. Methods (trends, simulation), 4. Results, 5. Comparison with the paper, 6. Limitations.

stuck.label: I'm not sure what limitations to write
hints: Which assumption in your simulation would you most like to test if you had more time?
Limitations name the assumptions and data choices that could change your conclusions, such as independent errors between years, a single dataset, and the version of the data.
Analogous example: a survey report says who was asked, who was not, and what might change if others had been asked. Write the same three things about your temperature analysis.

stuck.label: I'm worried my conclusion is too strong
hints: Does your result describe the global average, or does it say something about any single city or country?
Careful conclusions state what was measured, with which data and method, and how certain the result is. Words like 'likely' should match the probabilities you computed.
Sentence skeleton: 'Using GISTEMP v4 data downloaded on ___ and ___ simulated histories, we estimate that ___ was the warmest year so far with a probability of about ___, assuming ___.'

quiz.question: Which pandas option treats a symbol such as '***' as a missing value when reading a CSV?
quiz.explanation: na_values lists strings that pandas should read as missing (NaN).

quiz.question: How do you select only the years from 1980 onward in a DataFrame with a 'year' column?
quiz.explanation: Boolean indexing with a condition inside df[...] keeps the matching rows.

quiz.question: A temperature anomaly is best described as:
options: The difference from an average over a reference period
The highest temperature of a year
quiz.explanation: Anomalies compare each value with a baseline average.

quiz.question: Why do global records use anomalies instead of raw temperatures?
options: They let stations in very different climates be combined fairly
quiz.explanation: A mountain station and a coastal station have different raw temperatures but comparable changes.

quiz.question: A linear fit of anomaly against year gives a slope in degrees per year. How do you express it per decade?
quiz.explanation: A decade is ten years, so the per-year rate times ten is the per-decade rate.

quiz.question: Why should every trend be reported with its start and end years?
options: Trends change depending on the period chosen
quiz.explanation: The same data can give different slopes over different periods.

quiz.question: What does a Monte Carlo simulation do?
options: Finds the exact answer without randomness
Repeats a calculation many times with random inputs to see the range of outcomes
quiz.explanation: It estimates probabilities and spreads by sampling many random cases.

quiz.question: For a normally distributed error, a 95% interval spans roughly how many standard deviations on each side?
quiz.explanation: About 1.96 standard deviations on each side cover 95% of a normal distribution.

guides.why: Read the temperature table, clean it and make plots.
guides.summary: pandas stores tables as DataFrames. You can read a CSV file while skipping title lines, mark symbols as missing values, select columns and filter rows by a condition, then plot the result.
steps: Read a CSV with skiprows and na_values
guides.practice: Load any small CSV with a title line and a missing-value symbol, and plot one column over time.

guides.why: GISTEMP reports differences from a reference period, not raw temperatures.
guides.summary: An anomaly is how much a value differs from an average over a chosen reference period. Climate records use anomalies because changes are more comparable across places than raw temperatures. Changing the baseline shifts all anomalies by the same amount but does not change trends.
steps: Compute an anomaly by subtracting a baseline mean
See that a new baseline shifts the curve but keeps its shape
Explain why stations are combined as anomalies
guides.practice: Take five daily temperatures, compute their mean, and write each day as an anomaly from that mean.

guides.why: You will measure how fast temperature changed over different periods.
guides.summary: A linear trend is the slope of the straight line that best fits the data. It summarizes the average rate of change over a period, but it depends on the period chosen and can hide changes in speed.
steps: Fit a straight line with numpy.polyfit
Read the slope and its units
Plot the data with the fitted line
guides.practice: Fit lines to the first half and the second half of any time series and compare the two slopes.

guides.why: You will simulate many possible histories from each year's uncertainty to estimate probabilities.
guides.summary: Uncertainty describes how far the true value might be from the reported one. Monte Carlo simulation draws many random versions of the data within that uncertainty, and the share of versions where something happens estimates its probability.
steps: Learn the normal distribution and standard deviation
Convert a 95% interval into a standard deviation
Count outcomes across simulations to estimate a probability
guides.practice: Simulate 10,000 rolls of two dice and estimate how often the sum is at least 10.
